question: Where do we stand, and what does syncing with zeroclaw master actually cost?
headline: The upstream sync is applied. 23 upstream commits are merged, the four moved anchors are re-pointed at the new protocol crate, the three exhaustiveness constraints upstream imposes are satisfied, and the fork's tracked core is byte-identical to upstream master again. The cargo sweep that followed the merge failed five tests in three targets; a control run against pristine upstream sorted them, and the three the fork owned are fixed. The tree now fails exactly what pristine upstream fails.
verdict: The sync is in, and the fork is back at parity with upstream. The tracked core matches byte for byte, the overlay follows upstream's structure in zeroclaw-rpc-proto, and release.json pins the base the core actually matches. The sweep that the merge triggered also surfaced three real defects in the consolidated tool families — the overlay was promising a tool a default build cannot deliver, and was offering the memory family to runs that had removed the memory tools. Both are fixed and gated. What is left is the CI gap: upstream's Quality Gate still does not run in the fork, so nothing checks those anchors for us.

triage.headline: Five failures in three cargo targets, sorted by a control run against pristine upstream.
triage.method: The sweep that followed the merge failed three targets. To tell a regression from an inherited failure, a second worktree was created at upstream/master — pristine, no overlay, its own target directory — and the same sweep was run against it on the same machine. A failure that reproduced there is upstream's; a failure that did not is the fork's.
triage.after: 3 failures in 2 targets — exactly the three pristine upstream fails

rows.cause: The inventory row a family gets claimed Always while its members sit behind tools-external. The email family collapses two external adapters, so a default build promised a tool it cannot deliver, and upstream's gate — every compiled row must register under the maximal config — failed on the missing family.
rows.fix: The row now carries the compilation group of the family's members, and a family that collects the external adapters joins the canonical adapter list beside them, so upstream's "the external compilation rows match the canonical adapter names" check holds.

rows.cause: The scope filter drops the persistent memory tools by name, and a family's own name is not one of its members'. A memory-free cron run was therefore still offered the memory family, whose description names every member and whose actions call the very tools uses_memory = false removes. This was a behavioural defect, not only a test failure: the run was offered memory access it had been told to drop.
rows.fix: A consolidated family is now offered only while at least one of its members is, and the builtin-selection fixture follows the same rule for the ACP turn.

rows.cause: The fixture the overlay maintains expected the memory family to survive the ACP turn even though every member was dropped — the old behaviour, written down.
rows.fix: The fixture now drops a family whose every member is a memory tool, so the expectation states the corrected rule.

triage.note: The overlay gate grew from 27 to 35 tests. The new ones state the two rules the fixes rest on: a family row has to carry its members' compilation group, and no family may mix memory and other members, carry a tool the filter drops by itself, or be a member of another family — so the family lookup terminates.

anchors.surviving: All 44 anchors now resolve exactly once — the four moved ones at their new homes in zeroclaw-rpc-proto, and the other 40 where they were: the authz and MethodAuthz arms in dispatch.rs, the handle_session_state insertion point, tool_names in agent.rs and the tool-result status field in zeroclaw-api/src/agent.rs.
anchors.resolved: Each moved anchor was re-pointed at upstream's own structure rather than reshaping it. The enum variant, the wire-name entry and a new Method::contract arm now live in zeroclaw-rpc-proto/src/method.rs; SessionToolsResult and the tool-result status field live in zeroclaw-rpc-proto/src/types.rs; and SessionToolsResult joins the proto schema catalog, because upstream's rule is that plain wire data lives in the protocol crate and the catalog is exclusive.

hidden_risks.title: The consolidation promised a tool a build cannot deliver
hidden_risks.detail: Every consolidated family got an inventory row claiming Always, while the email family's members sit behind tools-external. A default build therefore promised a tool it could not deliver, and upstream's own gate — every compiled row must register under the maximal config — failed on it. The row now carries the compilation group of the members, and a family that collects the external adapters joins the canonical adapter list with them.

hidden_risks.title: The consolidation offered memory to runs that had removed it
hidden_risks.detail: The scope filter drops the persistent memory tools by name, and a family's own name is not one of its members'. A cron run with uses_memory = false was therefore still offered the memory family, whose description names every member and whose actions call the very tools the run was told to drop. This was behaviour, not only a test: the run was offered memory access it had been denied. A family is now offered only while at least one of its members is, and the overlay gate states that rule.

hidden_risks.title: Upstream's CI never runs the desktop crate — the fork does
hidden_risks.detail: upstream's ci.yml excludes zeroclaw-desktop from every test job, so upstream never runs apps/tauri's own tests. The fork's Desktop App Check does, which is how a one-off ubuntu-22.04 failure in spawn_daemon_kills_group_when_supervisor_exits_before_cleanup surfaced. The code is byte-identical to upstream, and the same commit passed on re-run; a standalone reproducer built from upstream's own functions did not reproduce it in 620 Linux iterations — including under CPU starvation — or 300 macOS ones. The fork is the first place this test runs, so this is where it will be seen.

hidden_risks.title: Method::contract is arm-complete — satisfied
hidden_risks.detail: upstream's contract() match covers the closed enum exhaustively — its own comment says a new method cannot be added without declaring what it accepts and returns. The overlay now adds the SessionTools arm in zeroclaw-rpc-proto/src/method.rs, alongside the variant. The crate compiles and the contract test passes.

hidden_risks.title: Method::ALL is the single wire table — satisfied
hidden_risks.detail: wire_name() panics with "every variant is in ALL" if a variant is missing from the table, and from_wire() is a scan of that same table. The session/tools entry lands in the table in zeroclaw-rpc-proto/src/method.rs, not only in the enum.

hidden_risks.title: The schema catalog test is exclusive — satisfied
hidden_risks.detail: every_typed_contract_resolves_to_a_schema_or_an_external_owner asserts a named contract type is EXACTLY ONE of catalog-defined or external. SessionToolsResult is added to the proto catalog — it is plain data, so upstream's own rule puts it in the protocol crate. The test passes.

hidden_risks.title: The overlay now patches a published crate
hidden_risks.detail: zeroclaw-rpc-proto is publish = true and its rpc_type! macro derives JsonSchema under schema-export, where the runtime's macro does not. The fork's added success field on the tool-result notification now participates in schema export. The tracked OpenRPC document stays upstream's, so upstream's own cargo generate openrpc --check still passes against the tracked crate — editing the generated document by hand would break that gate. The prepared tree's copy is stale by exactly the session/tools method, and the book is not part of the shipped release artifact.

hidden_risks.title: Upstream's Quality Gate still does not run in the fork
hidden_risks.detail: upstream's ci.yml triggers only on pull_request to master while the fork's default branch is enact/branding — so upstream's Quality Gate does not run here at all, and the merge brought in a new gate inside it (cargo generate openrpc --check). Only Validate PR title, Apply path labels and the manually dispatched native build run on the fork's PRs. Retargeting the gate at enact/branding is a decision about CI minutes, so it is left to the owner.

hidden_risks.title: The release gate check — now clean
hidden_risks.detail: AGENTS.md requires git diff --exit-code $upstream_base -- src crates Cargo.toml Cargo.lock with the base pinned in release.json. That check failed before the sync: release.json pinned 1c1cd118 while the branch's core actually matched 06765b1e6, 75 upstream commits further on. release.json now pins 2c0a8c263 and the check passes clean.

hidden_risks.title: The distribution version — moved
hidden_risks.detail: The merge takes Cargo.toml to 0.9.0, so release.json's version moved from 0.8.7-enact.2 to 0.9.0-enact.1 and the upstreamCommit pin became the new upstream head. The published 0.8.7-enact.1 release and its withdrawn sibling stay untouched.

rules.detail: In adl-tan-theta/enact-agent. The zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw upstream is the source that gets reviewed and merged in, never the destination. Recorded in overlays/enact/AGENTS.md (commit 2dea86718) and in the enact-tools README.
Upstream master is the source of truth for the core. The fork owns the overlay; upstream owns the Rust. A sync is a merge plus an anchor re-point, never a rewrite of upstream's structure.

rules.rule: The overlay never edits tracked Rust
rules.detail: All native changes are authored under overlays/enact/ and injected by build.py into the prepared tree. No new crates, no Cargo.toml or Cargo.lock churn, cargo build --locked.

open: Upstream's Quality Gate still does not run in the fork: ci.yml triggers on pull_request to master, and the fork's default branch is enact/branding. The merge brought a new gate inside it (cargo generate openrpc --check). Retargeting it is a decision about CI minutes, so it is left to the owner.
The native build workflow is still manual only (workflow_dispatch), so no PR is gated by a native build automatically.

The prepared tree's OpenRPC document is stale by exactly the session/tools method. The tracked document stays upstream's so upstream's own --check stays green, and the book is not part of the shipped release artifact.
The 0.9.0-enact.1 distribution has not been cut or published. The published 0.8.7-enact.1 release is untouched.

Three cargo tests still fail on this machine — two relay::local_dial_tests cases that cannot stall a macOS loopback connect, and one order-dependent model-routing case. All three fail the same way on a pristine upstream/master worktree, and the files involved are byte-identical to upstream.
One upstream desktop test failed once on ubuntu-22.04 in the fork's Desktop App Check and passed on re-run. Upstream's own CI never runs that crate, so the fork is where this test is seen at all.
